idiom_name: logging.Handler subclass chaining hmac.new over the canonicalised record
implementation_notes: The standard library supplies both halves: subclass logging.Handler (or wrap a logging.FileHandler) and implement emit() to canonicalise the record with a trusted timestamp, chain hmac.new(key, prev + seq + body, sha256), and append the authenticator with the record; hmac.compare_digest is the verification primitive on the reading side. The classic hand-written writer is justified when the audit stream must be independent of the logging hierarchy - for instance records inserted into the same database transaction as the change they describe.
code_sketch:
class SecureAuditHandler(logging.Handler):
    def __init__(self, key, path):
        super().__init__()
        self._key, self._prev, self._seq = key, b"", 0
        self._fh = open(path, "ab", buffering=0)          # append-only, one writer process
    def emit(self, record):
        body = canonical(record)                          # stable order, redacted, %-args resolved
        msg = self._prev + self._seq.to_bytes(8, "big") + body
        tag = hmac.new(self._key, msg, hashlib.sha256).digest()
        self._fh.write(tag + b" " + body + b"\n"); os.fsync(self._fh.fileno())
        self._prev, self._seq = tag, self._seq + 1
pitfalls: logging.Handler.handle() serialises emit() only within one process: two worker processes appending to the same file fork the chain, so give the chain a single owner (or a dedicated writer process) and open the file O_APPEND in binary mode.
json.dumps key order, float repr and Unicode normalisation are the verifier's problem too - pin the serialiser (sort_keys, separators, encoding) in one module used by both writer and verifier.
logging.Formatter may already have interpolated secrets or CRLF into record.msg; canonicalise from record.__dict__ with an explicit allow-list and never log str(record.args) verbatim.
